claim: Only a subset of cancer patients respond to T-cell checkpoint inhibitors.
source: Only a subset of cancer patients respond to T-cell checkpoint inhibitors, highlighting the need for alternative immunotherapeutics.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical outcomes that is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: CRISPR-Cas9 screens were performed in a leukemia cell line to identify perturbations that enhance natural killer effector functions.
source: We performed CRISPR-Cas9 screens in a leukemia cell line to identify perturbations that enhance natural killer effector functions.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach taken in the study.

claim: The screens defined critical components of the tumor-immune synapse.
source: Our screens defined critical components of the tumor-immune synapse and highlighted the importance of cancer cell interferon-γ signaling in modulating NK activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the screening data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The screens highlighted the importance of cancer cell interferon-γ signaling in modulating NK activity.
source: Our screens defined critical components of the tumor-immune synapse and highlighted the importance of cancer cell interferon-γ signaling in modulating NK activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the screening data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disrupting the ubiquitin ligase substrate adaptor DCAF15 strongly sensitized cancer cells to NK-mediated clearance.
source: Surprisingly, disrupting the ubiquitin ligase substrate adaptor DCAF15 strongly sensitized cancer cells to NK-mediated clearance.
evidence: This is a finding from the CRISPR screens and validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: DCAF15 disruption induced an inflamed state in leukemic cells, including increased expression of lymphocyte costimulatory molecules.
source: DCAF15 disruption induced an inflamed state in leukemic cells, including increased expression of lymphocyte costimulatory molecules.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and flow cytometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cohesin complex members were endogenous client substrates of DCAF15.
source: Proteomic and biochemical analysis revealed that cohesin complex members were endogenous client substrates of DCAF15.
evidence: This is based on BioID proximity ligation and ubiquitination assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic disruption of DCAF15 was phenocopied by treatment with indisulam.
source: Genetic disruption of DCAF15 was phenocopied by treatment with indisulam, an anticancer drug that functions through DCAF15 engagement.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing similar immunophenotypic changes with DCAF15 knockout and indisulam treatment.

claim: Indisulam is an anticancer drug that functions through DCAF15 engagement.
source: Genetic disruption of DCAF15 was phenocopied by treatment with indisulam, an anticancer drug that functions through DCAF15 engagement.
evidence: This is based on published literature cited in the manuscript (Han et al., 2017; Uehara et al., 2017).

claim: In AML patients, reduced DCAF15 expression was associated with improved survival.
source: In AML patients, reduced DCAF15 expression was associated with improved survival.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA and TARGET AML patient datasets presented in the manuscript.

claim: DCAF15 inhibition may have useful immunomodulatory properties in the treatment of myeloid neoplasms.
source: These findings suggest that DCAF15 inhibition may have useful immunomodulatory properties in the treatment of myeloid neoplasms.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings and patient data.

claim: Treatment response to checkpoint inhibitors is positively correlated with tumor mutational burden.
source: Treatment response is positively correlated with tumor mutational burden and infiltration of CD8+ effector T cells, which recognize tumor cells via peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecules, suggesting that checkpoint inhibitors work best at clearing highly immunogenic cancers with repressed T cell responses (Snyder et al., 2014; Tumeh et al., 2014; Mariathasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Treatment response to checkpoint inhibitors is positively correlated with infiltration of CD8+ effector T cells.
source: Treatment response is positively correlated with tumor mutational burden and infiltration of CD8+ effector T cells, which recognize tumor cells via peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecules, suggesting that checkpoint inhibitors work best at clearing highly immunogenic cancers with repressed T cell responses (Snyder et al., 2014; Tumeh et al., 2014; Mariathasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CD8+ effector T cells recognize tumor cells via peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecules.
source: Treatment response is positively correlated with tumor mutational burden and infiltration of CD8+ effector T cells, which recognize tumor cells via peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecules, suggesting that checkpoint inhibitors work best at clearing highly immunogenic cancers with repressed T cell responses (Snyder et al., 2014; Tumeh et al., 2014; Mariathasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology.

claim: Checkpoint inhibitors work best at clearing highly immunogenic cancers with repressed T cell responses.
source: Treatment response is positively correlated with tumor mutational burden and infiltration of CD8+ effector T cells, which recognize tumor cells via peptides bound to major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) molecules, suggesting that checkpoint inhibitors work best at clearing highly immunogenic cancers with repressed T cell responses (Snyder et al., 2014; Tumeh et al., 2014; Mariathasan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference supported by cited literature.

claim: B2M and JAK1/2 mutations have been identified in melanoma patients with acquired resistance to checkpoint inhibitors.
source: B2M and JAK1/2 mutations have been identified in melanoma patients with acquired resistance to checkpoint inhibitors (Zaretsky et al., 2016; Sade-Feldman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: B2M and JAK1/2 mutations impair recognition of the tumor by the adaptive immune system.
source: These mutations impair recognition of the tumor by the adaptive immune system, either by directly disrupting antigen presentation or by rendering the cells insensitive to IFNγ, an important inducer of MHC-I expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of these genes and cited literature.

claim: IFNγ is an important inducer of MHC-I expression.
source: These mutations impair recognition of the tumor by the adaptive immune system, either by directly disrupting antigen presentation or by rendering the cells insensitive to IFNγ, an important inducer of MHC-I expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunology.

claim: Functional genetic screens using T cell-cancer cell cocultures have highlighted mechanisms of resistance to immune control in vitro.
source: Functional genetic screens using T cell-cancer cell cocultures have highlighted similar mechanisms of resistance in vitro (Kearney et al., 2018; Pan et al., 2018; Manguso et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Treatment-naïve tumors can be highly immuno-edited, presenting with IFNγ pathway mutations, reduced MHC-I expression and loss of peptide sequences that can serve as antigens.
source: Even treatment-naïve tumors can be highly immuno-edited, presenting with IFNγ pathway mutations, reduced MHC-I expression and loss of the peptide sequences that can serve as antigens (Dunn et al., 2004; Rodig et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2016; McGranahan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: There is a critical need for therapies that can either increase MHC expression or work in a MHC-independent fashion.
source: Together, these findings highlight a critical need for therapies that can either increase MHC expression or work in a MHC-independent fashion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current therapies described in the preceding text.

claim: Natural killer (NK) cells can have both direct tumoricidal activity and help to fully elaborate long-lasting anti-tumor responses.
source: Innate immune cells, most notably natural killer (NK) cells, can have both direct tumoricidal activity and also help to fully elaborate long-lasting anti-tumor responses (Marcus et al., 2014; Moynihan et al., 2016; Lopez-Soto et al., 2017; Chiossone et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NK cells are cytotoxic lymphocytes capable of mounting rapid responses to damaged, infected, or stressed cells, including cancer cells.
source: NK cells are cytotoxic lymphocytes capable of mounting rapid responses to damaged, infected, or stressed cells, including cancer cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: T and NK cells share effector functions, releasing cytokines and exocytosing lytic granules upon activation to kill target cells.
source: T and NK cells share effector functions, releasing cytokines and exocytosing lytic granules upon activation to kill target cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about lymphocyte biology.

claim: NK activation status is controlled by the integrated signals from germline-encoded NK-activating and -inhibiting receptors (aNKRs/iNKRs).
source: However, NK activation status is controlled by the integrated signals from germline-encoded NK-activating and -inhibiting receptors (aNKRs/iNKRs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: iNKR ligands are generally expressed by normal and healthy cells.
source: Generally, iNKR ligands are expressed by normal and healthy cells, whereas aNKR ligands are upregulated after DNA damage or viral insult (Chiossone et al., 2018; Ljunggren and Malmberg, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: aNKR ligands are upregulated after DNA damage or viral insult.
source: Generally, iNKR ligands are expressed by normal and healthy cells, whereas aNKR ligands are upregulated after DNA damage or viral insult (Chiossone et al., 2018; Ljunggren and Malmberg, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: MHC-I molecules provide a potent inhibitory signal sensed by NK cells.
source: MHC-I molecules provide a potent inhibitory signal sensed by NK cells, enabling the innate immune system to respond productively to MHC-deficient cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: The innate immune system can respond productively to MHC-deficient cells.
source: MHC-I molecules provide a potent inhibitory signal sensed by NK cells, enabling the innate immune system to respond productively to MHC-deficient cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NK cell biology.

claim: There is considerable interest in amplifying NK responses to cancers and developing NK-based cell therapies.
source: As a result, there is considerable interest in amplifying NK responses to cancers, as well as developing NK-based cell therapies (Lopez-Soto et al., 2017; Chiossone et al., 2018; Ljunggren and Malmberg, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Genetic screens were performed in an MHC-deficient leukemic cell line to systematically identify modulators of NK-mediated anti-cancer immunity.
source: Here, we performed genetic screens in an MHC-deficient leukemic cell line to systematically identify modulators of NK-mediated anti-cancer immunity.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach of the study.

claim: The screens revealed the potential therapeutic utility of targeting DCAF15 in myeloid malignancies.
source: These screens, unexpectedly, revealed the potential therapeutic utility of targeting the cullin4-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase (CRL4) substrate adaptor DCAF15 in myeloid malignancies.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the screening and validation data.

claim: Disruption of DCAF15 strongly sensitized cancer cells to NK-mediated killing, resulting from increased cancer cell expression of lymphocyte costimulatory molecules.
source: Disruption of DCAF15 strongly sensitized cancer cells to NK-mediated killing, resulting from increased cancer cell expression of lymphocyte costimulatory molecules.
evidence: This is based on competitive co-culture assays and flow cytometry data.

claim: DCAF15 interacted with and promoted the ubiquitination of cohesin complex members.
source: Proteomic experiments revealed that DCAF15 interacted with and promoted the ubiqitination of the cohesin complex members.
evidence: This is based on BioID proximity ligation and ubiquitination assays.

claim: Treatment with indisulam reduced interaction with cohesin members and mimicked DCAF15 loss-of-function immunophenotypes.
source: Treatment with indisulam, an anticancer drug that modulates DCAF15 function, reduced interaction with cohesin members and mimicked DCAF15 loss-of-function immunophenotypes.
evidence: This is based on BioID and flow cytometry experiments with indisulam treatment.

claim: K562 human chronic myelogenous leukemia cells are a NK-sensitive cancer cell line that weakly expresses MHC-I.
source: K562 human chronic myelogenous leukemia cells are a NK-sensitive cancer cell line that weakly expresses MHC-I.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the K562 cell line.

claim: NK-92 cells are a human lymphoma-derived cell line phenotypically similar to activated NK cells.
source: NK-92 cells are a human lymphoma-derived cell line phenotypically similar to activated NK cells (Klingemann et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NK-92 cells exhibit interleukin-2 (IL-2)-dependent growth.
source: These cells exhibit interleukin-2 (IL-2)-dependent growth, express a large number of aNKRs and few iNKRs (Maki et al., 2001), and display potent cytolytic activity against K562 cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NK-92 cells express a large number of aNKRs and few iNKRs.
source: These cells exhibit interleukin-2 (IL-2)-dependent growth, express a large number of aNKRs and few iNKRs (Maki et al., 2001), and display potent cytolytic activity against K562 cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: NK-92 cells display potent cytolytic activity against K562 cells.
source: These cells exhibit interleukin-2 (IL-2)-dependent growth, express a large number of aNKRs and few iNKRs (Maki et al., 2001), and display potent cytolytic activity against K562 cells.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Disruption of ICAM1 was the top-ranked NK-92 evasion mechanism in the screen.
source: Disruption of ICAM1 was the top-ranked NK-92 evasion mechanism, scoring many orders of magnitude stronger than any other gene—an observation consistent with the critical role of ICAM1-LFA1 interactions in establishing initial target-lymphocyte adhesion and polarizing cytotoxic granules towards the synapse (Marcus et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the screening data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ICAM1-LFA1 interactions play a critical role in establishing initial target-lymphocyte adhesion and polarizing cytotoxic granules towards the synapse.
source: Disruption of ICAM1 was the top-ranked NK-92 evasion mechanism, scoring many orders of magnitude stronger than any other gene—an observation consistent with the critical role of ICAM1-LFA1 interactions in establishing initial target-lymphocyte adhesion and polarizing cytotoxic granules towards the synapse (Marcus et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Single guide RNAs targeting NCR3LG1 were enriched after NK-92 challenge.
source: Single guide RNAs targeting multiple other tumor-immune synapse components were also enriched after NK-92 challenge, including NCR3LG1 (#26-ranked gene by MaGeCK score), the activating ligand for NKP30 on NK cells (Brandt et al., 2009); CD58 (#37), an adhesion molecule that binds CD2 (Selvaraj et al., 1987; Rölle et al., 2016); and CD84 (#80), a SLAM-related receptor that binds homotypically to promote activation and cytokine secretion in lymphocytes (Martin et al., 2001; Veillette, 2006; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the screening data.

claim: NCR3LG1 is the activating ligand for NKP30 on NK cells.
source: Single guide RNAs targeting multiple other tumor-immune synapse components were also enriched after NK-92 challenge, including NCR3LG1 (#26-ranked gene by MaGeCK score), the activating ligand for NKP30 on NK cells (Brandt et al., 2009); CD58 (#37), an adhesion molecule that binds CD2 (Selvaraj et al., 1987; Rölle et al., 2016); and CD84 (#80), a SLAM-related receptor that binds homotypically to promote activation and cytokine secretion in lymphocytes (Martin et al., 2001; Veillette, 2006; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: CD58 is an adhesion molecule that binds CD2.
source: Single guide RNAs targeting multiple other tumor-immune synapse components were also enriched after NK-92 challenge, including NCR3LG1 (#26-ranked gene by MaGeCK score), the activating ligand for NKP30 on NK cells (Brandt et al., 2009); CD58 (#37), an adhesion molecule that binds CD2 (Selvaraj et al., 1987; Rölle et al., 2016); and CD84 (#80), a SLAM-related receptor that binds homotypically to promote activation and cytokine secretion in lymphocytes (Martin et al., 2001; Veillette, 2006; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CD84 is a SLAM-related receptor that binds homotypically to promote activation and cytokine secretion in lymphocytes.
source: Single guide RNAs targeting multiple other tumor-immune synapse components were also enriched after NK-92 challenge, including NCR3LG1 (#26-ranked gene by MaGeCK score), the activating ligand for NKP30 on NK cells (Brandt et al., 2009); CD58 (#37), an adhesion molecule that binds CD2 (Selvaraj et al., 1987; Rölle et al., 2016); and CD84 (#80), a SLAM-related receptor that binds homotypically to promote activation and cytokine secretion in lymphocytes (Martin et al., 2001; Veillette, 2006; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: sgRNAs targeting NK-inhibitory surface proteins did not score prominently as NK-sensitization mechanisms, except for NECTIN2.
source: Other than NECTIN2, sgRNAs targeting NK-inhibitory surface proteins did not score prominently as NK-sensitization mechanisms, consistent with the weak MHC-I expression on K562 cells and the limited repertoire of NK inhibitory receptors expressed on NK-92 cells (Maki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is based on the screening data and is consistent with known properties of K562 and NK-92 cells.

claim: NECTIN2 transmits both stimulatory or inhibitory signals to NK cells, depending on whether it is bound to DNAM1 (CD226) or TIGIT, respectively.
source: NECTIN2 transmits both stimulatory or inhibitory signals to NK cells, depending on whether it is bound to DNAM1 (CD226) or TIGIT, respectively (Stanietsky et al., 2009; Bottino, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: After ICAM1, the top 10 highest scoring NK-92 evasion mechanisms were dominated by sgRNAs targeting the proximal components of the IFNγ signaling pathway.
source: After ICAM1, the top 10 highest scoring NK-92 evasion mechanisms were dominated by sgRNAs targeting the proximal components of the IFNγ signaling pathway, including STAT1, JAK1, IFNGR2, JAK2 and INFGR1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the screening data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: sgRNAs targeting negative regulators of the interferon response were strongly depleted after NK-92 challenge.
source: Consistent with the importance of cancer cell IFNγ signaling, sgRNAs targeting negative regulators of the interferon response were strongly depleted after NK-92 challenge.
evidence: This is based on the screening data.

claim: Disruption of PTPN2 was the #2 ranked NK-92-sensitizing mechanism.
source: Disruption of the protein tyrosine phosphatases PTPN2 and PTPN1 were the #2 and #5 ranked NK-92 -sensitizing mechanisms, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the screening data.

claim: Disruption of PTPN1 was the #5 ranked NK-92-sensitizing mechanism.
source: Disruption of the protein tyrosine phosphatases PTPN2 and PTPN1 were the #2 and #5 ranked NK-92 -sensitizing mechanisms, respectively.
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the screening data.

claim: PTPN2 and PTPN1 suppress IFNγ-induced immunomodulation by dephosphorylating STAT and JAK proteins.
source: Presumably, these proteins suppress IFNγ-induced immunomodulation by dephosphorylating STAT and JAK proteins, as has been reported in CRISPR screens using T-cell coculture systems or syngeneic tumor models (Pan et al., 2018; Manguso et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The top-ranked mechanism for promoting NK-92 mediated clearance was disruption of DCAF15.
source: Most surprisingly, the top-ranked mechanism for promoting NK-92 mediated clearance was disruption of DCAF15, an uncharacterized substrate adaptor for CRL4 ubiquitin E3 ligases.
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the screening data.

claim: DCAF15 is an uncharacterized substrate adaptor for CRL4 ubiquitin E3 ligases.
source: Most surprisingly, the top-ranked mechanism for promoting NK-92 mediated clearance was disruption of DCAF15, an uncharacterized substrate adaptor for CRL4 ubiquitin E3 ligases.
evidence: This is a characterization of DCAF15 based on existing knowledge.

claim: DCAF15 is a member of the large family of DDB1 and Cul4-associated factors (DCAFs).
source: DCAF15 is a member of the large family of DDB1 and Cul4-associated factors (DCAFs) (Jin et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: CRL4 complexes enable cells to mark proteins for proteosomal degradation, helping regulate intracellular protein homeostasis.
source: CRL4 complexes enable cells to mark proteins for proteosomal degradation, helping regulate intracellular protein homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CRL4 complexes.

claim: DCAF proteins provide specificity to CRL4 complexes, determining which client proteins are ubiquitinated.
source: As substrate adaptors for CRL4, DCAF proteins provide specificity to the complex, determining which client proteins are ubiquitinated (Jackson and Xiong, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The normal client repertoire of DCAF15 is undefined.
source: As with most substrate adaptors, the normal client repertoire of DCAF15 is undefined, and relatively little is known about the biological function of DCAF15.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Disruption of STAG2 scored as a NK-92 sensitization factor (ranked #26).
source: We also noted that disruption of two cohesin-related genes, STAG2 and HDAC8, scored as NK-92 sensitization factors (ranked #26 and #19, respectively).
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the screening data.

claim: Disruption of HDAC8 scored as a NK-92 sensitization factor (ranked #19).
source: We also noted that disruption of two cohesin-related genes, STAG2 and HDAC8, scored as NK-92 sensitization factors (ranked #26 and #19, respectively).
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the screening data.

claim: Cohesin is a ring-shaped complex involved in chromatin replication, organization and repair.
source: Cohesin is a ring-shaped complex involved in chromatin replication, organization and repair, with STAG2 acting as a core complex member and HDAC8 controlling chromatin accessibility (Uhlmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: STAG2 acts as a core cohesin complex member.
source: Cohesin is a ring-shaped complex involved in chromatin replication, organization and repair, with STAG2 acting as a core complex member and HDAC8 controlling chromatin accessibility (Uhlmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: HDAC8 controls chromatin accessibility.
source: Cohesin is a ring-shaped complex involved in chromatin replication, organization and repair, with STAG2 acting as a core complex member and HDAC8 controlling chromatin accessibility (Uhlmann, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Cohesin dysregulation has cell context-specific consequences, including DNA damage and aneuploidy.
source: Cohesin dysregulation has cell context-specific consequences, including DNA damage and aneuploidy; in leukemic cells, cohesin mutations are thought to enforce stem cell programs by altering chromatin organization (Mazumdar and Majeti, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In leukemic cells, cohesin mutations are thought to enforce stem cell programs by altering chromatin organization.
source: Cohesin dysregulation has cell context-specific consequences, including DNA damage and aneuploidy; in leukemic cells, cohesin mutations are thought to enforce stem cell programs by altering chromatin organization (Mazumdar and Majeti, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: MHC-I levels are highly upregulated in K562 cells after IFNγ exposure, increasing 5.9+/- 0.98 fold after 24 hr.
source: MHC-I levels are highly upregulated in K562 cells after IFNγ exposure, increasing 5.9+ /- 0.98 fold after 24 hr of exposure to IFNγ.
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry measurements presented in the manuscript.

claim: IFNγ-induced MHC-I upregulation in K562 cells is dependent on STAT1.
source: This induction was dependent on STAT1 and was nearly doubled by disrupting PTPN2 (Figure 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: IFNγ-induced MHC-I upregulation in K562 cells is nearly doubled by disrupting PTPN2.
source: This induction was dependent on STAT1 and was nearly doubled by disrupting PTPN2 (Figure 2A–B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Cells with impaired MHC-I upregulation were highly enriched for sgRNAs targeting the IFNγ-JAK-STAT pathway.
source: As expected, cells with impaired MHC-I upregulation were highly enriched for sgRNAs targeting the IFNγ-JAK-STAT pathway (IFNGR1/2, JAK1/2, STAT1, IRF1/2), as well as the antigen processing/presentation machinery (B2M, TAP1/2, TAPBP, PDIA3, HLA-C/B) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the MHC-I upregulation screen shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Cells with impaired MHC-I upregulation were highly enriched for sgRNAs targeting the antigen processing/presentation machinery.
source: As expected, cells with impaired MHC-I upregulation were highly enriched for sgRNAs targeting the IFNγ-JAK-STAT pathway (IFNGR1/2, JAK1/2, STAT1, IRF1/2), as well as the antigen processing/presentation machinery (B2M, TAP1/2, TAPBP, PDIA3, HLA-C/B) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on the MAGeCK analysis of the MHC-I upregulation screen shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Disruption of PTPN2 or STAG2 induced an exuberant MHC-I response.
source: Conversely, disruption of PTPN2 or STAG2 induced an exuberant MHC-I response.
evidence: This is based on the MHC-I upregulation screen data.

claim: sgRNAs targeting epigenetic factors were highly enriched within the brightest MHC-I expressing cells.
source: Surprisingly, sgRNAs targeting epigenetic factors were highly enriched within the brightest MHC-I expressing cells—most prominently, members of the BCOR complex PCGF1 and KDM2B, members of the PRC2 complex EZH2 and SUZ12, as well as factors affecting histone methylation/acetylation status.
evidence: This is based on the MHC-I upregulation screen data.

claim: Comparing sgRNAs enriched after NK-92 challenge with those causing impaired MHC-I upregulation clearly delineated the known proximal components of the IFNγ signaling pathway.
source: Comparing sgRNAs enriched after NK-92 challenge with those causing impaired MHC-I upregulation clearly delineated the known proximal components of the IFNγ signaling pathway (IFNGR1/2, JAK1/2, STAT1), and highlighted several poorly characterized genes such as GSE1, SPPL3 and NR2F2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on the rank-rank comparison shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Comparing sgRNAs depleted after NK-92 challenge with those causing an exaggerated MHC-I response highlighted DCAF15 most prominently, alongside STAG2 and HDAC8.
source: Surprisingly, comparing sgRNAs depleted after NK-92 challenge with those causing an exaggerated MHC-I response highlighted the CRL4 substrate adaptor DCAF15 most prominently, alongside the cohesin members STAG2 and HDAC8 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on the rank-rank comparison shown in Figure 2E.

claim: DCAF15 KO K562 cells displayed 2.45-fold higher levels of MHC-I than control knockout cells after 24 hr of IFNγ exposure.
source: Consistent with the screening results, polyclonal K562 cells expressing DCAF15 sgRNAs ('DCAF15 KO cells') displayed 2.45-fold higher levels of MHC-I than control knockout cells after 24 hr of IFNγ exposure, an effect comparable in magnitude to PTPN2 disruption (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DCAF15 KO cells did not show differences in induction of STAT1 phosphorylation after IFNγ exposure.
source: We were unable to see any difference in induction of STAT1 phosphorylation after IFNγ exposure in DCAF15 KO cells, or differences in steady state levels of STAT1/2, JAK1/2 or IFNGR1 (Figure 4B and data not shown).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: DCAF15 KO cells appeared healthy and proliferated at a normal rate.
source: DCAF15 KO cells appeared healthy and proliferated at a normal rate (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on cell growth measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Long-term IFNγ exposure was neither cytotoxic nor cytostatic to DCAF15 KO cells.
source: As in wild-type K562 cells, long-term IFNγ exposure was neither cytotoxic nor cytostatic to DCAF15 KO cells (Figure 4c and Chen et al., 1986).
evidence: This is based on cell growth data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PTPN2 KO cells showed higher levels of STAT1PY701 induction after IFNγ exposure.
source: In contrast, PTPN2 KO cells showed higher levels of STAT1PY701 induction after IFNγ exposure, and their proliferative rate was temporarily reduced after transient exposure to IFNγ, or more substantially slowed down by continuous treatment with the cytokine (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is based on western blot and cell growth data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: PTPN2 KO cells' proliferative rate was temporarily reduced after transient exposure to IFNγ.
source: In contrast, PTPN2 KO cells showed higher levels of STAT1PY701 induction after IFNγ exposure, and their proliferative rate was temporarily reduced after transient exposure to IFNγ, or more substantially slowed down by continuous treatment with the cytokine (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is based on cell growth data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PTPN2 KO cells' proliferative rate was more substantially slowed down by continuous treatment with IFNγ.
source: In contrast, PTPN2 KO cells showed higher levels of STAT1PY701 induction after IFNγ exposure, and their proliferative rate was temporarily reduced after transient exposure to IFNγ, or more substantially slowed down by continuous treatment with the cytokine (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is based on cell growth data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PTPN2 KO cells were transcriptionally distinct from control or DCAF15 KO cells both before and after cytokine exposure.
source: Clustering analysis clearly showed that PTPN2 KO cells were transcriptionally distinct from control or DCAF15 KO cells both before and after cytokine exposure (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the basal state, PTPN2 KO cells were enriched for inflammation and interferon-associated Gene Ontology (GO) terms.
source: In the basal state, PTPN2 KO cells were enriched for inflammation and interferon-associated Gene Ontology (GO) terms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: After cytokine exposure, PTPN2 KO cells had exaggerated transcriptional responses to interferon and were enriched for apoptotic GO gene categories.
source: After cytokine exposure, gene set enrichment analysis revealed that PTPN2 KO cells had exaggerated transcriptional responses to interferon and were also enriched for apoptotic GO gene categories (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on gene set enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: PTPN2 KO cells showed greater IFNγ-induced MHC-I and ICAM1 cell surface expression.
source: PTPN2 KO cells also showed greater IFNγ-induced MHC-I and ICAM1 cell surface expression (Figure 2A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DCAF15 KO cells did not show substantial differences in their transcriptional response to IFNγ.
source: In contrast, DCAF15 KO cells did not show substantial differences in their transcriptional response to IFNγ (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on principal component analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: DCAF15 KO cells were enriched for GO terms associated with NK-mediated cytotoxicity, antigen presentation and cell adhesion.
source: However, DCAF15 KO cells were enriched for GO terms associated with NK-mediated cytotoxicity, antigen presentation and cell adhesion, consistent with our phenotypic characterization of these cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: CD80 was one of the most significantly upregulated genes in DCAF15 KO K562 cells.
source: Intriguingly, differential expression analysis showed that one of the most significantly upregulated genes in DCAF15 KO K562 cells was CD80 (Figure 4F; Q value 3.7e-23, Beta value 0.98).
evidence: This is based on differential expression analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CD80 is an important co-stimulatory molecule for lymphocytes, regulating T cell activation and tolerance by ligation to CD28, CTLA4 or PDL1.
source: CD80 is an important co-stimulatory molecule for lymphocytes, regulating T cell activation and tolerance by ligation to CD28, CTLA4 or PDL1 (Chen and Flies, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: During antigen-presenting cell (APC) activation, the upregulation of MHC molecules and CD80 provide critical antigenic and costimulatory signals to T cells.
source: During antigen-presenting cell (APC) activation, the upregulation of MHC molecules and CD80 provide critical antigenic and costimulatory signals to T cells (Acuto and Michel, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: K562 cells are an undifferentiated and multipotential CML cell line, well-studied for their ability to differentiate towards many different lineages, including APC-like states.
source: K562 cells are an undifferentiated and multipotential CML cell line, well-studied for their ability to differentiate towards many different lineages, including APC-like states (Lindner et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Immunophenotyping of unstimulated DCAF15 KO cells revealed higher levels of CD80, CD40, MHC-I, and MHC-II.
source: Indeed, immunophenotyping of unstimulated DCAF15 KO cells revealed higher levels of the APC markers CD80, CD40 as well as class I and II MHC molecules (Figure 5A; 2.23-fold CD80 increase; 2.01-fold CD40 increase; 1.44-fold MHC-I increase; 1.22-fold MHC-II increase).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: DCAF15 KO cells did not display higher levels of the APC maturation marker CD83.
source: DCAF15 KO cells did not display higher levels of the APC maturation marker CD83 (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The changes to the DCAF15 KO cell immunophenotype could be rescued by constitutive expression of a sgRNA-resistant DCAF15 open-reading frame.
source: Importantly, the changes to the DCAF15 KO cell immunophenotype could be rescued by constitutive expression of a sgRNA-resistant DCAF15 open-reading frame (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Transducing tumors with the B7 ligands CD80 or CD86 can enhance anti-tumor immunity by enabling the tumor cells to directly deliver antigenic and costimulatory signals to T and NK cells.
source: Transducing tumors with the B7 ligands CD80 or CD86 can enhance anti-tumor immunity by enabling the tumor cells to directly deliver antigenic and costimulatory signals to T and NK cells (Townsend and Allison, 1993; Chen et al., 1992; Wilson et al., 1999; Galea-Lauri et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: B7 ligands have been shown to promote NK activation, via CD28-dependent and -independent pathways.
source: While best understood in the context of T cell biology, B7 ligands have been shown to promote NK activation, via CD28-dependent and -independent pathways (Wilson et al., 1999; Galea-Lauri et al., 1999; Chambers et al., 1996; Azuma et al., 1992; Martín-Fontecha et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: NK-92 cells are CD28-positive.
source: We confirmed that NK-92 cells are CD28-positive, whereas we could not detect CD28 on peripheral CD3- CD56+ NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: CD28 could not be detected on peripheral CD3- CD56+ NK cells.
source: We confirmed that NK-92 cells are CD28-positive, whereas we could not detect CD28 on peripheral CD3- CD56+ NK cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Over-expression of wild-type CD80 was sufficient to increase K562 sensitivity to NK-92 mediated killing.
source: Over-expression was sufficient to increase K562 sensitivity to NK-92 mediated killing (Figure 5C), whereas overexpression of a mutant form of CD80 carrying point mutations that abrogate CD28 binding (Peach et al., 1995) (CD80Q65A,M72A) had no effect.
evidence: This is based on competitive co-culture data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Overexpression of a mutant form of CD80 carrying point mutations that abrogate CD28 binding had no effect on K562 sensitivity to NK-92 mediated killing.
source: Over-expression was sufficient to increase K562 sensitivity to NK-92 mediated killing (Figure 5C), whereas overexpression of a mutant form of CD80 carrying point mutations that abrogate CD28 binding (Peach et al., 1995) (CD80Q65A,M72A) had no effect.
evidence: This is based on competitive co-culture data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: ICAM1 KO cells triggered less NK-92 degranulation than control cells (by 52 ± 12%).
source: As expected, ICAM1 KO cells triggered less NK-92 degranulation than control cells (by 52 ± 12%) and were not significantly affected by CD80 antagonism (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on CD107 flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ICAM1 KO cells were not significantly affected by CD80 antagonism.
source: As expected, ICAM1 KO cells triggered less NK-92 degranulation than control cells (by 52 ± 12%) and were not significantly affected by CD80 antagonism (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on CD107 flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: DCAF15 KO cells showed a 17 ± 8% increased ability to trigger NK-92 cells.
source: DCAF15 KO cells showed a 17 ± 8% increased ability to trigger NK-92 cells and were approximately twice as sensitive to CD80 antagonism compared to control cells (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is based on CD107 flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: DCAF15 KO cells were approximately twice as sensitive to CD80 antagonism compared to control cells.
source: DCAF15 KO cells showed a 17 ± 8% increased ability to trigger NK-92 cells and were approximately twice as sensitive to CD80 antagonism compared to control cells (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is based on CD107 flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Following CD80 antagonism, degranulation triggered by DCAF15 KO was not significantly different from untreated control cells.
source: Following CD80 antagonism, degranulation triggered by DCAF15 KO was not significantly different from untreated control cells.
evidence: This is based on CD107 flow cytometry data.

claim: Aryl sulfonamide drugs have demonstrated promising anti-cancer properties in hematological malignancies.
source: Aryl sulfonamide drugs have demonstrated promising anti-cancer properties in hematological malignancies (Assi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Aryl sulfonamide drugs work by binding DCAF15 and redirecting the ubiquitination activity of the CRL4-DCAF15 E3 ligase towards the essential splicing factor RBM39.
source: Recently, it was discovered that these agents work by binding DCAF15 and redirecting the ubiquitination activity of the CRL4-DCAF15 E3 ligase towards the essential splicing factor RBM39 (Han et al., 2017; Uehara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mechanism of action of aryl sulfonamides is conceptually similar to that of the 'IMiD' thalidomide analogs.
source: This mechanism of action is conceptually similar to that of the 'IMiD' thalidomide analogs, which promote the degradation of various lymphocyte transcription factors by engaging the CRL4-cereblon E3 ubiquitin ligase (Ito et al., 2010; Fischer et al., 2014; Krönke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to published literature.

claim: IMiD thalidomide analogs promote the degradation of various lymphocyte transcription factors by engaging the CRL4-cereblon E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: This mechanism of action is conceptually similar to that of the 'IMiD' thalidomide analogs, which promote the degradation of various lymphocyte transcription factors by engaging the CRL4-cereblon E3 ubiquitin ligase (Ito et al., 2010; Fischer et al., 2014; Krönke et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: K562 cells were sensitive to indisulam.
source: Three-day dose-response experiments revealed that K562 cells were sensitive to indisulam, and that DCAF15 disruption reduced this sensitivity, consistent with previous reports (Uehara et al., 2017) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on dose-response data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: DCAF15 disruption reduced K562 sensitivity to indisulam.
source: Three-day dose-response experiments revealed that K562 cells were sensitive to indisulam, and that DCAF15 disruption reduced this sensitivity, consistent with previous reports (Uehara et al., 2017) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on dose-response data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There is a positive relationship between DCAF15 mRNA expression levels and indisulam sensitivity across a panel of hematological cancer cell lines.
source: Dose-response experiments across a panel of 16 hematological cancer cell lines confirmed the reported positive relationship between DCAF15 mRNA expression levels and indisulam sensitivity (Han et al., 2017) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A; R2 = 0.33, p=0.02).
evidence: This is based on dose-response and expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 100 nM indisulam treatment moderately lowered RBM39 levels while minimally affecting cell viability and proliferation over a four-day period.
source: We empirically determined that 100 nM indisulam treatment moderately lowered RBM39 levels while minimally affecting cell viability and proliferation over a four-day period (Figure 6C-D and Uehara et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on western blot and cell growth data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: 100 nM indisulam treatment was able to recapitulate the increased CD80 expression seen in K562 DCAF15 KO cells (2.14-fold increase).
source: Remarkably, this treatment regime was able to recapitulate the increased CD80 expression seen in K562 DCAF15 KO cells (Figure 6E; 2.14-fold increase), and more modestly, the effects on MHC-I and CD40 expression (1.36-fold and 1.27-fold increase, respectively).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 100 nM indisulam treatment modestly increased MHC-I expression (1.36-fold) and CD40 expression (1.27-fold) in K562 cells.
source: Remarkably, this treatment regime was able to recapitulate the increased CD80 expression seen in K562 DCAF15 KO cells (Figure 6E; 2.14-fold increase), and more modestly, the effects on MHC-I and CD40 expression (1.36-fold and 1.27-fold increase, respectively).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CD80 upregulation by indisulam was first detected 24 hr after treatment initiation and plateaued after 48 hr.
source: CD80 upregulation was first detected 24 hr after treatment initiation and plateaued after 48 hr (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry time-course data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Indisulam treatment did not further upregulate CD80 in K562 DCAF15 KO cells.
source: Importantly, indisulam treatment did not further upregulate CD80 in K562 DCAF15 KO cells, suggesting that the pharmaco-modulation of CD80 levels was entirely mediated through DCAF15 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The pharmaco-modulation of CD80 levels by indisulam was entirely mediated through DCAF15.
source: Importantly, indisulam treatment did not further upregulate CD80 in K562 DCAF15 KO cells, suggesting that the pharmaco-modulation of CD80 levels was entirely mediated through DCAF15 (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that indisulam does not further increase CD80 in DCAF15 KO cells.

claim: Both Daudi and KU812 cells up-regulated CD80 levels after indisulam treatment (2.45-fold for Daudi, 1.71-fold for KU812).
source: Both Daudi and KU812 cells up-regulated CD80 levels after indisulam treatment (Figure 6G; 2.45-fold for Daudi, 1.71-fold for KU812).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Indisulam was not able to induce de novo CD80 expression in CD80-negative cell lines.
source: Indisulam was not able to induce de novo CD80 expression in CD80-negative cell lines (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is based on flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In both adult and pediatric AML, lower expression of DCAF15 mRNA was associated with increased median overall survival time.
source: In both adult and pediatric AML, lower expression of DCAF15 mRNA was associated with increased median overall survival time (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: This is based on Kaplan-Meier analysis of TCGA and TARGET AML datasets shown in Figure 6H-I.

claim: The improved survival of DCAF15-low patients was not driven by a correlation between DCAF15 expression and more aggressive AML subtypes.
source: The improved survival of DCAF15-low patients was not driven by a correlation between DCAF15 expression and more aggressive AML subtypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F–G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of AML subtypes shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: DCAF15 was fused to a promiscuous bacterial biotin ligase and stably expressed in K562 cells for proximity-based proteomic analysis.
source: DCAF15 was fused to a promiscuous bacterial biotin ligase (Roux et al., 2012) ('DCAF15-BioID') and stably expressed in K562 cells, enabling recovery of interaction partners by streptavidin pull-down.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach for identifying DCAF15 interaction partners.

claim: Exogenous C-terminally tagged DCAF15 was able to rescue DCAF15 KO phenotypes and associate with CRL4 complex members DDB1 and CUL4A.
source: We first confirmed that exogenous C-terminally tagged DCAF15 was able to rescue DCAF15 KO phenotypes and associate with CRL4 complex members DDB1 and CUL4A (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on rescue experiments and immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The basal concentration of biotin in the media (~3 μM) was sufficient to induce BioID activity in the absence of exogenous (50 μM) biotin supplementation during stable DCAF15 overexpression.
source: During stable DCAF15 overexpression, we observed that the basal concentration of biotin in the media (~3 μM) was sufficient to induce BioID activity in the absence of exogenous (50 μM) biotin supplementation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Proteasome inhibition by MG132 increased accumulation of DCAF15-BioID and biotinylated species.
source: However, proteasome inhibition by MG132 increased accumulation of DCAF15-BioID and biotinylated species.
evidence: This is based on western blot data.

claim: GFP-BioID accumulated much more readily than DCAF15-BioID, and its biotinylation activity was not affected by MG132 treatment.
source: GFP-BioID accumulated much more readily than DCAF15-BioID, and its biotinylation activity was not affected by MG132 treatment.
evidence: This is based on western blot data.

claim: Quantitative mass spectrometry clearly recovered DCAF15 and the core CRL4 complex, including DDA1, DDB1 and CUL4A.
source: This approach clearly recovered DCAF15 and the core CRL4 complex, including DDA1, DDB1 and CUL4A (DCAF15: 155.6-fold change, p=2.5e-152; DDA1: 24.5-fold change, p=6.5e-139; DDB1: 4.86-fold change, p=8.1e-21; CUL4A: 3.8-fold change, p=8.5e-18).
evidence: This is based on quantitative mass spectrometry data.

claim: Two of the most differentially biotinylated proteins were the cohesin complex members SMC1A and SMC3.
source: Surprisingly, two of the most differentially biotinylated proteins were the cohesin complex members SMC1A and SMC3 (SMC1: 2.39-fold change, p=0.00098; SMC3: 2.76-fold change, p=5e-5).
evidence: This is based on quantitative mass spectrometry data.

claim: The interaction between DCAF15-BioID and endogenous SMC1 and 3 was confirmed by streptavidin-pulldown followed by western blotting.
source: We confirmed the interaction between DCAF15-BioID and endogenous SMC1 and 3 by streptavidin-pulldown followed by western blotting (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: DCAF16-BioID fusions accumulated similarly to DCAF15-BioID, interacted with DDB1 but did not biotinylate SMC proteins.
source: When stably expressed in K562 cells, DCAF16-BioID fusions accumulated similarly to DCAF15-BioID, interacted with DDB1 but did not biotinylate SMC proteins (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Indisulam treatment led to substantial indisulam-dependent biotinylation of RBM39 and reduced recovery of biotinylated SMC proteins.
source: This treatment regime lead to substantial indisulam-dependent biotinylation of RBM39 and reduced recovery of biotinylated SMC proteins (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Co-expression of DCAF15, but not GFP, led to the recovery of poly-ubiquitinated SMC1A.
source: Co-expression of DCAF15, but not GFP, led to the recovery of poly-ubiquitinated SMC1A (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is based on nickel affinity chromatography and western blot data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Treatment with indisulam reduced the amount of ubiquitinated SMC1A recovered.
source: Treatment with indisulam reduced the amount of ubiquitinated SMC1A recovered.
evidence: This is based on nickel affinity chromatography and western blot data.

claim: Cohesin proteins are bona fide client ubiquitination substrates for DCAF15.
source: These orthogonal proteomic and biochemical assays support the notion that cohesin proteins are bona fide client ubiquitination substrates for DCAF15, with these interactions impaired by DCAF15-engaging aryl sulfonamide drugs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the BioID and ubiquitination assay data.

claim: Interactions between DCAF15 and cohesin are impaired by DCAF15-engaging aryl sulfonamide drugs.
source: These orthogonal proteomic and biochemical assays support the notion that cohesin proteins are bona fide client ubiquitination substrates for DCAF15, with these interactions impaired by DCAF15-engaging aryl sulfonamide drugs.
evidence: This is based on the BioID data showing reduced SMC biotinylation with indisulam treatment.

claim: Disrupting optimal antigen presentation levels is a common mechanism by which cancer cells escape recognition by the adaptive immune system.
source: Clinical and experimental data have revealed that disrupting optimal antigen presentation levels is a common mechanism by which cancer cells escape recognition by the adaptive immune system.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the literature discussed in the introduction.

claim: Disruption of DCAF15 or PTPN2 sensitizes a variety of cancer cell types to both NK-92 and primary NK cells.
source: We discovered and characterized how disruption of DCAF15 or PTPN2 sensitizes a variety of cancer cell types to both NK-92 and primary NK cells.
evidence: This is based on the competitive co-culture and degranulation assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The screens clearly identified known lymphocyte adhesion factors and aNKR/iNKR ligands, such as ICAM1, NCR3LG1, CD58, CD84 and NECTIN2.
source: In addition, the screens clearly identified known lymphocyte adhesion factors and aNKR/iNKR ligands, such as ICAM1, NCR3LG1, CD58, CD84 and NECTIN2.
evidence: This is based on the screening data.

claim: Performing additional genetic screens on diverse cancer cell lines and natural killer subtypes will enable a more complete understanding of the relative importance of various aNKRs and iNKRs and should identify novel immunotherapeutic targets.
source: Performing additional genetic screens on diverse cancer cell lines and natural killer subtypes will enable a more complete understanding of the relative importance of various aNKRs and iNKRs and should identify novel immunotherapeutic targets.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Disruption of PTPN2 consistently enhanced NK cell sensitivity.
source: We determined that disruption of PTPN2, a negative regulator of IFNγ signaling, consistently enhanced NK cell sensitivity.
evidence: This is based on the competitive co-culture and degranulation assays.

claim: Preventing cancer cell IFNγ signaling had a much more variable effect than removing negative feedback on the pathway, promoting resistance or sensitization to NK cells in target and effector cell dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, preventing cancer cell IFNγ signaling had a much more variable effect than removing negative feedback on the pathway, promoting resistance or sensitization to NK cells in target and effector cell dependent manner.
evidence: This is based on the competitive co-culture assays with STAT1 KO cells.

claim: In K562 cells, PTPN2 KO rendered IFNγ treatment growth suppressive, likely through the induction of apoptosis.
source: In K562 cells, PTPN2 KO rendered IFNγ treatment growth suppressive, likely through the induction of apoptosis, while also enhancing the immunomodulatory effects of the cytokine.
evidence: This is based on cell growth and RNA-seq data showing enrichment of apoptotic gene categories.

claim: PTPN2 disruption has previously been shown to enhance activated T-cell mediated killing, as well as potentiate the effect of immunotherapy in syngeneic tumor models.
source: PTPN2 disruption has previously been shown to enhance activated T-cell mediated killing, as well as potentiate the effect of immunotherapy in syngeneic tumor models (Pan et al., 2018; Manguso et al., 2017; Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Targeting PTPN2 may be a generalizable strategy to sensitize tumor cells to multiple arms of the immune system.
source: These data suggest that targeting PTPN2 may be a generalizable strategy to sensitize tumor cells to multiple arms of the immune system.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the data presented and cited literature.

claim: DCAF15 KO cells did not have a grossly dysregulated response to IFNγ, but scored in the MHC-I screen due to higher unstimulated levels of MHC-I.
source: We determined that DCAF15 KO cells did not have a grossly dysregulated response to IFNγ, but scored in the MHC-I screen due to higher unstimulated levels of MHC-I.
evidence: This is based on western blot and flow cytometry data.

claim: Higher CD80 levels in DCAF15 KO cells were especially important for increasing NK-92 cell triggering.
source: Higher CD80 levels in DCAF15 KO cells were especially important for increasing NK-92 cell triggering.
evidence: This is based on CD80 blocking experiments and CD80 overexpression experiments.

claim: Cross-talk between APCs and NK cells is a well-established phenomenon that mutually regulates both cell types.
source: Cross-talk between APCs and NK cells is a well-established phenomenon that mutually regulates both cell types (Ferlazzo and Münz, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: APC-NK interactions can promote APC maturation or lysis in a context-dependent fashion.
source: These interactions, which often occur at sites of inflammation or secondary lymphoid organs, can promote APC maturation or lysis in a context-dependent fashion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about APC-NK interactions.

claim: The surface factors upregulated by DCAF15 disruption are not direct client proteins of the substrate receptor, but rather represent events secondary to altered turnover of the normal DCAF15 client protein(s).
source: Our data suggest that the surface factors upregulated by DCAF15 disruption are not direct client proteins of the substrate receptor, but rather represent events secondary to altered turnover of the normal DCAF15 client protein(s).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data showing cohesin as DCAF15 substrates.

claim: Rather than globally controlling SMC protein levels, CRL4-DCAF15 complexes likely ubiquitinate cohesin at specific genomic sites to regulate chromatin topology or repair.
source: Rather than globally controlling SMC protein levels, we speculate that CRL4-DCAF15 complexes ubiquitinate cohesin at specific genomic sites to regulate chromatin topology or repair (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the data.

claim: In this model, disruption of either STAG2, HDAC8 or DCAF15 impair cohesin function with overlapping phenotypic consequences.
source: In this model, disruption of either STAG2, HDAC8 or DCAF15 impair cohesin function with overlapping phenotypic consequences.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the screening data.

claim: The cytotoxic effects of indisulam were driven by splicing defects resulting from RBM39 degradation.
source: The cytotoxic effects of indisulam were driven by splicing defects resulting from RBM39 degradation.
evidence: This is based on published literature.

claim: Concentrations of indisulam with limited RBM39 degradation or cytotoxicity had immunomodulatory properties that phenocopied genetic DCAF15 disruption.
source: We also discovered indisulam-induced phenotypes attributable to inhibition of DCAF15's normal functions. Concentrations of indisulam with limited RBM39 degradation or cytotoxicity had immunomodulatory properties that phenocopied genetic DCAF15 disruption.
evidence: This is based on the low-dose indisulam experiments showing CD80 upregulation.

claim: The recruitment of endogenous client proteins to CRL4-DCAF15 and subsequent ubiquitination was impaired by indisulam treatment.
source: Biochemically, the recruitment of endogenous client proteins to CRL4-DCAF15 and subsequent ubiquitination was impaired by indisulam treatment.
evidence: This is based on the BioID and ubiquitination assay data with indisulam treatment.

claim: AML patients with naturally occurring lower levels of DCAF15 had improved overall survival.
source: We also determined that AML patients with naturally occurring lower levels of DCAF15 had improved overall survival.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA and TARGET AML datasets.

claim: The clinical data on DCAF15 expression and AML survival provide a rationale for drugging DCAF15 in myeloid neoplasms.
source: While these clinical data are preliminary in nature, they provide a rationale for drugging DCAF15 in myeloid neoplasms, achieved through judicious dosing of existing anti-cancer sulfonamides or the development of pure DCAF15 inhibitors.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the patient data and experimental findings.
